I am 75 years old now, and I have been farming these flat lands in Quzhou County since I was a young man. I only finished primary school, but I know this soil better than any book. I have about 6 mu of good land that my family has worked for generations. At my age, I do not chase new crops or risky experiments—my back is not what it used to be, and I rely on my son to help with the tractor and combine harvester when he is free from his factory job.

The start of the growing season means my winter wheat is already in the ground from last October. I will see it through to harvest in early June. Before sowing wheat last autumn, I used the rotary tiller to break up the soil after the maize stubble. For fertilizer, I apply urea and compound fertilizer to the wheat—about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus phosphate and potash. I will irrigate four times: the winter irrigation to help it survive the cold, then at green-up in spring, again at jointing, and once more at grain filling. I spray three times: herbicide once, and insecticide twice if the aphids show up.

As soon as the wheat is harvested in early June, I will plant summer maize immediately. I will not till the soil again; I direct-seed the hybrid denghai605 into the wheat stubble using the no-till planter. This saves diesel, saves labor, and the stubble keeps the moisture in the ground when the summer heat comes. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat—about 12 kg of nitrogen per mu, and a little phosphorus and potassium. I irrigate twice, right after sowing and at the big trumpet stage. I spray three times: herbicide, and insecticide for the corn borer.

I expect around 525 kg of wheat per mu and about 560 kg of maize per mu. That is not the highest yield in the village, but at my age, steady and reliable puts food on the table.
